title: Reduction of in utero lead exposures in South African populations: Positive impact of unleaded petrol.
ehr_evidence: Participants also consented to access and use of hospital birth outcome data (including maternal and neonate characteristics such as weight, length and head circumference, gestational age, Apgar score, as well as birth complications, if any) for research purposes. The actual data source was biological samples (maternal blood, urine, cord blood) and questionnaires.
summary: Assessment of in utero lead exposure and its association with birth outcomes in a large South African cohort following the legislative removal of lead from petrol.
key_findings: Overall, the geometric mean of maternal blood lead was 1.32 μg/dL (n = 640; 95% CI, 1.24–1.40).
In the subset cohort, paired maternal and cord blood lead levels were positively correlated (rho = 0.65, p < 0.001).
Geographical differences were found in gestational age (p<0.001), birth length (p=0.028), head circumference (p<0.001), Apgar score at 5 min (p<0.001), and parity (p<0.002).
In female neonates, cord blood lead was positively associated with head circumference (rho = 0.243; p<0.016).
No significant association was found between maternal blood lead and infant weight, length, or head circumference overall.
Multivariate analysis showed mothers who did not use pesticides at home had lower lead levels compared to those who did (β = -0.14; 95% CI, -0.26 to -0.02).
population: pregnant women and neonates in coastal regions of South Africa
limitations: cord blood samples limited to Indian Ocean sites only due to financial constraints
